questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the statement of comprehensive income?
options: The statement showing revenue, costs and profit over a period of time
The statement showing assets and liabilities at a single date
The statement showing cash received and paid during a period
The statement showing the shareholders on the register
questions.why: It reports performance across a period, which is why it is described as a film of the year rather than a photograph.
whyNot: That is the statement of financial position.
That is the statement of cash flows.
The share register is not a financial statement.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the statement of financial position?
options: The statement showing assets, liabilities and equity at a single date
The statement showing revenue and profit over a year
The statement showing dividends paid to shareholders
The statement showing forecast sales for next year
questions.why: It is a snapshot at one date, showing what the business owns, what it owes and how it is financed.
whyNot: That is the statement of comprehensive income.
Dividends appear within the statements but are not a statement in themselves.
Forecasts are internal planning documents, not published financial statements.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a current asset?
options: Trade receivables
A delivery vehicle
A long-term bank loan
Retained earnings
questions.why: Current assets are expected to become cash within a year, and trade receivables are amounts customers owe.
whyNot: A vehicle is held for more than a year, so it is a non-current asset.
A long-term loan is a non-current liability, not an asset.
Retained earnings form part of equity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-current liability?
options: A bank loan repayable in five years
An overdraft
Trade payables
Inventory
questions.why: Non-current liabilities are debts due after more than one year.
whyNot: An overdraft is repayable on demand, so it is a current liability.
Trade payables are due within a year, so they are current liabilities.
Inventory is a current asset.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines equity?
options: The owners' stake: share capital plus retained earnings and reserves
The total value of the business's non-current assets
The amount owed to lenders
The cash held in the bank at the year end
questions.why: Equity is what belongs to the owners after liabilities are deducted from assets.
whyNot: Non-current assets are only part of what the business owns.
Amounts owed to lenders are liabilities, not equity.
Cash is one current asset, not the owners' stake.

questions.stem: Which statement would a bank considering a loan look at most closely, and why?
options: The statement of financial position, because it shows gearing, liquidity and assets available as security
The statement of comprehensive income, because revenue growth proves the loan will be repaid
The share register, because it shows who owns the business
The mission statement, because it shows the business's intentions
questions.why: A lender wants to know the loan will be serviced and repaid, which depends on debt levels, liquidity and security rather than on sales growth.
whyNot: Revenue growth matters to shareholders far more than to a lender assessing repayment risk.
Ownership does not directly show ability to repay.
Intentions are not evidence of financial capacity.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder is most likely to use the statements to support a claim for higher pay?
options: Employees and their union
Suppliers
Customers
The local community
questions.why: A large reported profit is evidence that there is money available to share, which is exactly what a pay claim rests on.
whyNot: Suppliers are concerned with whether they will be paid.
Customers are mainly concerned with whether the business will survive to honour supply and warranties.
The community is concerned with employment and local impact.

questions.stem: A business reports a large investment in new non-current assets. How might a lender and a supplier read this differently?
options: The lender sees more security; the supplier worries about the cash consumed
Both see it as purely positive
Both see it as purely negative
Neither would be interested in it
questions.why: The same figure supports different conclusions depending on the reader's interest, which is the key evaluation point in this topic.
whyNot: A supplier may be concerned that cash has been tied up in assets rather than kept available to pay bills.
A lender generally welcomes assets that could serve as security.
Both have a direct interest in the business's financial position.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of published financial statements?
options: They contain no non-financial information such as morale, brand strength or innovation
They are not audited in any country
They are prepared before the year begins
They show only forecast figures
questions.why: Much of what determines competitiveness is absent from the statements, which is why a full assessment needs human resource and market data too.
whyNot: Published statements of larger companies are audited.
They are prepared after the period, reporting what happened.
They report actual historical figures, not forecasts.

questions.stem: Why is it said that the statement of financial position can be arranged to look better than the year as a whole?
options: It reports one single date, so balances can be managed around that date
It is published before the year ends
It excludes all liabilities
It uses forecast rather than actual figures
questions.why: Because it is a snapshot, a business can time receipts, payments and borrowing around the year end, which is known as window dressing.
whyNot: It is published after the year end, reporting the position on that date.
It includes both current and non-current liabilities.
The figures are actual, not forecast.

questions.stem: A business shows a healthy profit but a weak statement of financial position. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: Profitable sales have been made on credit, so cash and liquidity are poor while profit is high
Profit and financial position always move together, so this cannot happen
The business must have understated its revenue
The business has no non-current assets
questions.why: Profit is recorded when a sale is made, not when cash arrives, so a business can be profitable and short of cash at the same time.
whyNot: They measure different things over different time frames, so they can diverge easily.
Understating revenue would reduce reported profit, not raise it.
Having no non-current assets would not by itself create this pattern.

questions.stem: Why is a fall in profit not necessarily a sign of poor management?
options: It may result from deliberate investment or expansion whose returns come later
Profit figures are never accurate
Profit is not reported in the financial statements
A fall in profit always indicates fraud
questions.why: Context matters: a fall caused by planned spending on growth is very different from a fall caused by losing control of costs.
whyNot: Audited profit figures are reasonably reliable; the issue is interpretation.
Profit is a central figure in the statement of comprehensive income.
There is no basis for assuming fraud from a profit fall.

questions.stem: Why do aggregated figures in the financial statements limit their usefulness to managers?
options: Totals hide which products or regions are performing and which are not
Totals are always calculated incorrectly
Totals exclude all costs
Totals are only published every five years
questions.why: A single revenue or profit figure gives no guidance on where to act, which is why managers need segmented internal information.
whyNot: The arithmetic is not the problem; the level of detail is.
Costs are included in the income statement.
Published statements are annual.

questions.stem: A question asks you to assess a business's competitiveness. What would make the answer most complete?
options: Combining the financial statements with human resource measures and market information such as share and satisfaction
Using only the profit figure, because it summarises everything
Using only the ratios, because they remove the need for other data
Using only the mission statement, because it states the objectives
questions.why: Competitiveness has financial, human and market dimensions, and naming what else you would want to see shows you understand the limits of the data.
whyNot: Profit alone omits liquidity, gearing and everything non-financial.
Ratios rest on the same historical financial data and share its limitations.
A mission statement states intentions, not performance.

questions.stem: Which statement is described as a photograph rather than a film, and why does the distinction matter?
options: The statement of financial position, because it covers one date rather than a period
The statement of comprehensive income, because it covers one date rather than a period
Both, because both cover a single date
Neither, because both cover a period
questions.why: One date can be unrepresentative of the whole year, which is why the distinction is worth stating explicitly.
whyNot: The income statement covers a period, so it is the film.
The income statement covers a period, not a date.
The statement of financial position is prepared at one date.

questions.stem: Why should you use International Accounting Standards terminology in your answers?
options: The assessments use terms such as statement of financial position and trade receivables
The older terms are no longer understood by anyone
It increases the number of marks available for a question
It is required only in Accounting papers, not Business
questions.why: Using the current terminology, while recognising the older names, is what the papers expect.
whyNot: Older terms such as balance sheet are still widely understood; the point is consistency with the assessment.
Terminology does not change the marks available; it affects whether yours are awarded.
The Business specifications use the same terminology.
